Ryan Crandall: First, we believe full-spectrum oil is very important — across Betty's, Bubby's Baked, and InHouse we use a full-spectrum oil input because we believe there's benefit beyond just THC distillate. Beyond that, we want to add safe supplements in combination with cannabinoids to elicit desired effects. Whether it's three, four, or five cannabinoids, I'm not opposed, if testing shows that combination gets the best response. We haven't brought anything to market without multiple test cases and samples behind it, to get to what we believe is close to a perfect product.

Bryan Fields: And "test cases" means individuals actually consuming the product and comparing, like which gave a better night's sleep?

Ryan Crandall: Correct — not just one individual, but many.

Bryan Fields: That becomes an educational factor — someone buying a sleep edible has six different options with different cannabinoid ratios, so the emphasis falls back on the budtender to point them in the right direction. Is working with budtenders part of communicating why the trifecta matters more than just two cannabinoids?

Ryan Crandall: We do a good job training budtenders, but they're inundated with information and everyone claims their product is best. What ultimately works is trial. I've got a guy on my sales team in Massachusetts who's really sensitive to sugar and can't sleep after a gummy — no sleep gummies work for him. We came up with Micro Dose under Nature's Heritage, a vegan pill using CBN and homeopathic mushrooms, and he's getting better sleep than he has in years — partly no sugar, partly the formula, partly his body's chemistry. I've seen people sleep better on InHouse gummies than Betty's, too. Your suite of products should offer people an array of trusted options, and ultimately it comes down to trust over time — we've been on shelves for years because we listen to our customers. For example, we're adding magnesium to our sleep SKU right now — we're the number one sleep SKU in the state but still looking to improve. We started with a sleep SKU with melatonin, then added a second without melatonin, then a pain SKU without melatonin. We'll keep iterating.

Bryan Fields: That's focused R&D — you're not going to make an Adderall pill for me, Bryan.

Ryan Crandall: Correct, 100%.

Bryan Fields: Is there a sweet-spot balance between pushing the category forward and knowing when not to push too far?

Ryan Crandall: We push through campaigns and education, but ultimately our brand ambassadors — even doing a Betty's Eddies push — are identifying opportunities for Bubby's and Nature's Heritage too, having good conversations with customers and building relationships with budtenders so we're paying more attention than the competition. We believe budtenders are key, so we do a lot of micro-events — we just did a cannabis dinner a couple weeks ago pairing Nature's Heritage strains with a chef's dishes for about 80 customers. Doing five or six of those over a couple months across a market is really impactful — people get two or three hours to interact directly with our food scientists and really nerd out on the products.

Bryan Fields: You're building trust, putting a face to the name, like people who idolize a chef and eat anything they make.

Ryan Crandall: Right, and you're connecting it all together for people who want that connection.

Bryan Fields: Would you say it's fair that someone could take an energetic edible and expect to feel energized?

Ryan Crandall: It's interesting — I'm curious what will happen with THCV. Have you had experience with it, Bryan?

Bryan Fields: I love THCV, but only paired with THC.

Ryan Crandall: I had one with maybe a milligram of THC but 10-15 milligrams of THCV, and I noticed a real difference — I felt like I'd had a cup of coffee, and later that night, when I'd normally have quite an appetite, I had zero. Not an upset stomach, just no interest in eating. Definitely appetite suppression and some energy. I think that's just scratching the surface — I know others have had similar experiences with that cannabinoid.

Bryan Fields: I've had that too — I like THCV with THC because it gives a more euphoric feeling; I use it for socialization instead of alcohol. On the flip side, CBG makes me starving — out of control. I'm not totally sure why.

Ryan Crandall: That's funny — we actually have an LTO with CBG in it, and I had a similar experience having a tough time with food after.

Bryan Fields: People often ask me, as an edibles consumer, whether it's really possible to buy something for energy and feel energized, versus something for sleep and feel sleepy.

Ryan Crandall: I think so. Betty's has a product, Betty's Go, a watermelon chew, and I do feel it energizes people. A lot of the energy drinks coming out, like Red Bull-type products, certainly work — our Vibations has natural caffeine and guarana in it, and if I have one too late I struggle to sleep. Ours are certainly formulated to work.

Bryan Fields: And those aren't high in THC?

Ryan Crandall: They're all lower dose. We do have a high-dose watermelon Betty's, but the majority of our products are 5 or 10 milligrams, with minors in the low milligrams below that.

Bryan Fields: So you can feel comfortable you won't be "sucked into the couch" — my recommendation is always go low and slow.

Ryan Crandall: 100% — we're thoughtful about that too, because people don't just eat one. There's a responsible way to make products efficacious without making them like a Four Loko in one bite. For example, we put 1-2 milligrams of melatonin in our sleep products — 5-10 milligrams is an effective dose for a lot of people, but many feel overdosed at that level and get a strong effect from 1-2 milligrams. I haven't seen the edible side chase high milligram counts the way traditional CPG or pharma sometimes do — hopefully that doesn't happen, because effective doses are very specific to people on the edible side.

Bryan Fields: When you enter a new state, is there a brand you like to lead with, or does it depend on the state?

Ryan Crandall: If flower's available under the regulations, Nature's Heritage leads, alongside Betty's Eddies — those are our two marquee brands in any new market. If it's edibles-only, Betty's leads, with Bubby's Baked and InHouse. Betty's tends to open a lot of doors given how high-performing it is across markets, and dispensaries often covet it given its track record elsewhere.

Bryan Fields: Similar to how dispensaries know a brand can track consumers if it's performed well in other states.

Ryan Crandall: Right. It depends on the account too — some already have their assortment figured out, so Vibations is a good one to get in with because it's unique; a lot of accounts don't have a drink mix, and it's disruptive to the beverage category — a 10-pack for $20-25 at retail versus expensive individual cans. And with Bubby's, when you can say you're the number one baked good or number one powdered drink mix in the state, it lets our sales team ask an account, "why aren't you carrying the number one baked good in your state?" Saying that repeatedly, quarter over quarter, eventually erodes resistance from accounts that said no before.

Bryan Fields: Let's talk about Vibations — give us a high-level view of what it is and how to use it.

Ryan Crandall: Vibations is basically Liquid IV for cannabis people — a powdered drink mix in a small stick pack, sugar-free varieties a couple grams, sugar varieties 10-15 grams. You pour it into a bottle of water wherever you are. It's great for sporting events, concerts, or anywhere canned beverages, vapes, or pre-rolls aren't allowed — it lets a cannabis consumer discreetly dose anywhere responsibly. Feedback is a lot of active-lifestyle use — hikes, sporting events, workouts, concerts.

Bryan Fields: How many milligrams?

Ryan Crandall: Five milligrams in Massachusetts, 10 milligrams as a base in other states, with a variety of minor cannabinoid combinations. Most of the brand focuses on focus and energy, with some SKUs aimed at other effects.

Bryan Fields: I imagine that's a product where shipping cans would be expensive — does the powder format help unit economics?

Ryan Crandall: Some ingredients in the powders, like powderized THC, are costly, plus additional ingredient costs, but the economics get better as the brand grows. It's a good-margin product today, and I forecast it becoming even better as it scales.

Bryan Fields: Unit economics are such a dilemma in cannabis — siloing manufacturing state by state versus one central facility shipping out, especially with specialized packaging equipment like stick packs.

Ryan Crandall: Right, having that specialized equipment in each state can be a real barrier if you haven't accounted for those costs.

Bryan Fields: Coca-Cola isn't making 75 different packages for the Northeast — that'd be absurd — but in our industry it's normal.

Ryan Crandall: I know, it's crazy.

Bryan Fields: How do you think about the hemp industry? A lot of teams are moving into it — what's your appetite, and how do you plan to approach it?

Ryan Crandall: We're actively working on projects to expand our brands into the hemp space — cautiously, given news that may be coming down the pipe. There are interesting strategies around what minor cannabinoids might become available to general CPG businesses, and whether our brands link to that. A major benefit is brand-building — getting access to consumers in states where our regulated products aren't available. Our customers don't just shop in dispensaries; some don't like them or are scared to go in. We have to get our products to consumers responsibly wherever the law allows, holding the same standard for quality and testing regardless of channel.

Bryan Fields: Something like Vibations seems very shareable on social media — someone sees it discreetly used at a sporting event, wonders where to buy it, and it's available online — that can make a big difference quickly.

Ryan Crandall: Yes.

Bryan Fields: What area of the edibles market do you think most consumers are missing right now?

Ryan Crandall: It's interesting — the recent flash-in-the-pan hemp drink boom didn't seem to correlate to sales on the dispensary side. A lot of people are scratching their heads about why consumers weren't willing to buy those beverages in dispensaries at similar rates — is it a different customer base? I'm not sure. What's your theory?

Bryan Fields: I think it's because at the supermarket or liquor store, people are already in the mood to buy a beverage, so it competes directly with other drinks. At a dispensary, people walk in thinking "edible" or "flower," not necessarily "beverage" — those don't always seem to be the same customer mindset. I've seen friends in New York who bought THC drinks at the supermarket rather than a dispensary, specifically because they wanted something for someone who doesn't drink alcohol.

Ryan Crandall: That boom also opened people's eyes to feeling comfortable — smiling, relaxed, not feeling awful the next day. I'd love to see stats on how many people tried a cannabis beverage for the first time last Thanksgiving, and how that trend changes year over year. There's also the practical issue — dispensaries don't have shopping carts, they sell products one at a time, so buying six drinks looks a bit ridiculous and carrying out paper bags isn't convenient. But the appetite for cannabinoids being that massive shows we're just at the beginning of what I think will be a huge wave.

Bryan Fields: Last question — what question do you wish more people asked you?

Ryan Crandall: I wish people asked more about the team here — the amazing people across departments who've been so dedicated for so long on this journey. It gets me a little emotional; I love the people who've helped build what we're building, and they're going to be the future of this industry. I feel really passionate about the people who contribute here every day, and there are a whole lot of them.

Bryan Fields: Great answer. Ryan, for people who want to get in touch or buy your products, where can they find you?

Ryan Crandall: We're in Massachusetts, Maryland, Illinois, and Delaware with our products. We're also licensed in Maine, New York, and Rhode Island — not in New York yet, but we will be soon. We have retail stores in Massachusetts, Maryland, Illinois, Delaware, and Ohio.

Bryan Fields: Love it. Well, thanks for taking the time — this was a lot of fun.

Ryan Crandall: Thank you, Bryan.
summary: In this episode of The Dime, host Bryan Fields talks with Ryan Crandall, Chief Commercial Officer of MariMed, about how the multi-state cannabis operator builds consistent, high-quality edibles and flower products across a fragmented, state-by-state regulatory system. The conversation covers MariMed's brand portfolio (Betty's Eddies, Nature's Heritage, InHouse, Bubby's Baked, and Vibations), the behind-the-scenes R&D and testing processes used to standardize dosing and quality, the role of budtender education and in-store experiences in building trust, and emerging opportunities and challenges around cannabinoid drinks, THCV/CBG effects, hemp-derived products, and interstate expansion.
takeaways: MariMed centrally controls non-cannabis ingredients through proprietary 'bomb bags' to keep recipes consistent across every state it operates in.
Carrier oils are tested at multiple stages (raw oil, infused oil, and finished product) to ensure dosing accuracy, even though this isn't mandated in most states.
Consistent testing helps new labs in newly launched states calibrate faster and produces more reliable, repeatable results over time.
Consumer trust and repeat purchases, not just first-time sales, are the real measure of a successful cannabis brand.
MariMed's brand portfolio spans premium and value flower (Nature's Heritage, InHouse), edibles (Betty's Eddies, Bubby's Baked), and powdered cannabis drink mixes (Vibations).
Budtender education and in-person experiences like cannabis dinners are key channels for teaching consumers about dosing, cannabinoid blends, and product differences.
Minor cannabinoids like THCV and CBG can produce distinct, noticeable effects (energy/appetite suppression vs. increased appetite) that companies are beginning to formulate around.
Cannabis beverages sell differently in dispensaries versus liquor stores/supermarkets, suggesting a mismatch between where consumers are primed to buy drinks versus edibles or flower.

faq.question: How does MariMed keep edible and flower products consistent across multiple states?
faq.answer: MariMed centrally sources and pre-measures non-cannabis ingredients into what it calls 'bomb bags,' controlling recipes and processes from one location so that products made in different states follow the same disciplined formula and dosing standards.

faq.question: Is testing carrier oil before it goes into a cannabis product required by regulators?
faq.answer: No — according to Ryan Crandall, testing the raw and infused carrier oil before final product testing is generally not mandated by most states; MariMed does it voluntarily as an extra quality-control step to improve dosing accuracy.

faq.question: What was the early edibles market like in states such as Colorado?
faq.answer: In early legal markets like Colorado, some leading edible brands (such as Edipure) simply sprayed bulk convenience-store candy with cannabis oil, leading to inconsistent dosing and lower-quality products before more quality-focused brands emerged.

faq.question: What is a 'cannabinoid trifecta' in edibles?
faq.answer: It refers to combining three (or more) cannabinoids and full-spectrum oil in a single product formulation, tested through multiple consumer trials, to produce a more targeted and effective outcome (e.g., sleep, energy, pain relief) than THC alone.

faq.question: Why don't cannabis beverages sell as well in dispensaries as regular beverages sell in liquor stores?
faq.answer: One theory discussed is that consumers walking into a liquor store or supermarket are already in a 'buying a beverage' mindset, while dispensary customers are typically there to buy edibles or flower, making cannabis drinks a less natural purchase in that setting.

faq.question: What effects do THCV and CBG have according to this conversation?
faq.answer: THCV was described as producing an energizing, coffee-like effect along with appetite suppression, while CBG was described as significantly increasing appetite for at least one person interviewed — both illustrating how minor cannabinoids can produce distinct, noticeable effects.

faq.question: What is Vibations, MariMed's cannabis drink mix brand?
faq.answer: Vibations is a powdered, THC-infused drink mix sold in small stick packs (similar to Liquid IV or Crystal Light) that can be poured into any beverage, designed for discreet, portable dosing at events like concerts, hikes, or sporting events where cans or pre-rolls aren't allowed.

faq.question: How does MariMed decide which brand to lead with when entering a new state?
faq.answer: Nature's Heritage typically leads on the flower side and Betty's Eddies leads on the edibles side, since Betty's strong performance in other markets tends to make dispensaries eager to carry it, opening doors for the rest of MariMed's portfolio.

faq.question: Why does MariMed limit melatonin dosage in its sleep products?
faq.answer: Even though 5-10 milligrams of melatonin is a commonly effective dose, MariMed uses only 1-2 milligrams because many consumers report feeling overdosed or groggy at higher amounts, showing that effective cannabis/supplement dosing is highly individual.
